titleStmt.title: Somatostatin-Expressing Inhibitory Interneurons in Cortical Circuits
titleStmt.author: Yavorska
Wehr

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Somatostatin-Expressing Inhibitory Interneurons in Cortical Circuits

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: SOM cells in cerebral cortex, with an emphasis on mice
span.quote: In this review, we focus on SOM cells in cerebral cortex, with an emphasis on mice.

span.label: whether the classification criteria can vary independently or are correlated, which is what decides how many distinct subtypes there could be - and the assumptions are POORLY CONSTRAINED BY DATA BECAUSE MOST STUDIES HAVE MEASURED ONLY A SUBSET OF THESE CRITERIA
span.quote: Estimating such an upper bound requires several assumptions about whether classification criteria can vary independently (producing all possible combinations) or whether there are correlations that reduce the number of combinations. These assumptions are poorly constrained by data because most studies have measured only a subset of these criteria. In addition, we assume here that these criteria are static, although it's likely that some criteria could change over time.

span.label: an estimate of how many kinds of thing exist: THE TRUE NUMBER OF DISTINCT SUBTYPES OF SOM CELLS IS UNKNOWN, and it MOST LIKELY LIES SOMEWHERE BETWEEN 4 AND 100 SUBTYPES
span.quote: Thus while the true number of distinct subtypes of SOM cells is unknown, we estimate that it most likely lies somewhere between 4 and 100 subtypes.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Thus despite their heterogeneity and variability across cortical areas, current evidence shows that SOM neurons perform unique neural computations, forming not only distinct molecular but also functional subclasses of cortical inhibitory interneurons.

span.label: somatostatin-expressing cortical inhibitory interneurons
span.quote: Here, we review the function of somatostatin-expressing (SOM) inhibitory interneurons, focusing largely on sensory cortex.

span.label: review
span.quote: In this review, we focus on SOM cells in cerebral cortex, with an emphasis on mice.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Locomotion depolarizes VIP cells, which inhibit SOM cells, releasing neighbouring pyramidal neurons from SOM inhibition (disinhibition) and raising their gain
span.quote: These results suggest that the effect of locomotion is mediated by a disinhibitory circuit, in which VIP cells inhibit SOM cells and thereby increase the activity of neighboring PNs.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The same VIP-to-SOM disinhibitory motif, driven by M1 input during whisking, silences the tonically firing SOM cells of barrel cortex
span.quote: This disinhibitory circuit therefore explains how SOM cells cease their tonic firing and become hyperpolarized during whisking

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Weak facilitating excitatory input must be integrated over time before it reaches threshold, which is why SOM excitatory currents and spikes lag those of other cells
span.quote: Weak but facilitating input would take longer to integrate and produce a measurable EPSP, which could explain why excitatory currents in SOM cells are delayed.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: The spike threshold converts purely divisive subthreshold inhibition into an apparent narrowing of the spiking tuning curve
span.quote: Stronger suppression of PN spiking can narrow tuning curves, even with purely divisive inhibition, because of this effect of spike threshold

span.label: the count is built from combinations, not from observations: 2 MORPHOLOGICAL TYPES, potential combinations OF MOLECULAR MARKERS, and 2 FIRING-PROPERTY CLASSES, LEADING TO 256 POSSIBLE SUBTYPES OF SOM CELLS
span.quote: Thus there are 2 morphological types, 2 6 potential combinations of molecular markers, and 2 firing-property classes, leading to 256 possible subtypes of SOM cells

span.label: and the lower bound is built the other way, by naming four types that differ on every criterion at once - THIS ESTIMATE UNDOUBTEDLY LUMPS TOGETHER SUBTYPES OF CELLS THAT CAN BE DISTINGUISHED BY AT LEAST SOME CRITERIA, BUT REPRESENTS A LOWER BOUND
span.quote: At a minimum there are 4 distinct types: (1) L2/3 Martinotti cells, which are mostly regular-spiking, labeled by GIN, and target PNs, (2) L5 Martinotti cells, which include LTS, are labeled by X98, and target PNs, (3) L4 SOM cells, which are FS-like and target L4 PV+ cells, and some of which are labeled by X94, and (4) NOS/SPR long-projecting GABAergic cells that can make either cortico-cortical or corticofugal projections (Table 1 ). This estimate undoubtedly lumps together subtypes of cells that can be distinguished by at least some criteria, but represents a lower bound on the number of functionally distinct SOM subtypes.

span.label: SOM cells are RECRUITED by FACILITATING synapses rather than by thalamus, so they are unlikely to be recruited during periods of low cortical activity - the review's own summary of why the class behaves as a network
span.quote: It is important to remember that SOM cells are not a single population, but rather consist of several distinct classes of inhibitory cells

span.label: Because studies apply only partial and sometimes mutually exclusive classification methods, the number of combinatorial SOM subtypes cannot be settled.
span.quote: Because most studies have used only a subset of these categorization methods (indeed, some methods are mutually exclusive, such as the transgenic lines), it is still not clear how many distinct combinatorial types of SOM cells are found in the cerebral cortex.

span.label: The upper-bound estimate of ~100 subtypes rests on assumptions the data barely constrain.
span.quote: These assumptions are poorly constrained by data because most studies have measured only a subset of these criteria.

span.label: The role of SOM networks in learning is still largely open.
span.quote: Much remains to be understood about exactly how these SOM inhibitory networks are involved in learning.

span.label: Dense interneuron interconnectivity makes single-subtype perturbation experiments hard to interpret.
span.quote: Lastly, high levels of interconnectivity in cortical circuits make it challenging to study the effects of only a single interneuron subtype.

span.label: THE ASSUMPTIONS ARE POORLY CONSTRAINED BY DATA BECAUSE MOST STUDIES HAVE MEASURED ONLY A SUBSET OF THESE CRITERIA, and the criteria are assumed STATIC ALTHOUGH IT'S LIKELY THAT SOME CRITERIA COULD CHANGE OVER TIME
span.quote: Estimating such an upper bound requires several assumptions about whether classification criteria can vary independently (producing all possible combinations) or whether there are correlations that reduce the number of combinations. These assumptions are poorly constrained by data because most studies have measured only a subset of these criteria. In addition, we assume here that these criteria are static, although it's likely that some criteria could change over time.

span.label: the transgenic lines LABEL ONLY SUBSETS OF SOM CELLS, so ONE MUST BE CAREFUL NOT TO INFER RELATIVE PROPORTIONS OF SOM SUBTYPES FROM STUDIES USING THESE LINES
span.quote: But because they label only subsets of SOM cells, one must be careful not to infer relative proportions of SOM subtypes from studies using these lines.

span.label: the marker itself is not exact - ABOUT 5% OF GFP-EXPRESSING NEURONS IN THE X94 AND X98 LINES, AND 3% OF CELLS IN THE GIN LINE, ARE NOT SOM-POSITIVE
span.quote: It is also important to note that about 5% of GFP-expressing neurons in the X94 and X98 lines, and 3% of cells in the GIN line, are not SOM-positive

span.label: IMMUNOHISTOCHEMISTRY IS A RELATIVELY DIFFICULT TECHNIQUE, AND STANDARDS FOR ANTIBODY VALIDATION HAVE BEEN ADOPTED RELATIVELY RECENTLY, which LIKELY CONTRIBUTES TO SOMETIMES CONTRADICTORY RESULTS FOR PEPTIDE EXPRESSION IN DIFFERENT STUDIES
span.quote: More generally, it is important to note that immunohistochemistry is a relatively difficult technique, and standards for antibody validation have been adopted relatively recently. This likely contributes to sometimes contradictory results for peptide expression in different studies.

span.label: IT IS VIRTUALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO PERTURB THE ACTIVITY OF THE SOM NETWORK WITHOUT CHANGING FIRING PATTERNS IN OTHER INHIBITORY NEURONS, WHICH MAY LEAD TO CONFLICTING AND MISLEADING RESULTS
span.quote: Lastly, high levels of interconnectivity in cortical circuits make it challenging to study the effects of only a single interneuron subtype. In particular, it is virtually impossible to perturb the activity of the SOM network without changing firing patterns in other inhibitory neurons, which may lead to conflicting and misleading results

span.label: the suppression tool does not suppress evenly - SPONTANEOUS OR LOW-AMPLITUDE EVOKED ACTIVITY CAN SHOW 65-80% SUPPRESSION, WHEREAS STRONG EVOKED BURSTING ACTIVITY REMAINS UNCHANGED EVEN WITH HIGH-POWER ARCH ACTIVATION
span.quote: In the case of Arch-mediated suppression, for instance, depending on the cell type, and region of inactivation, it can be extremely difficult to completely silence neural responses. For example, spontaneous or low-amplitude evoked activity can show 65–80% suppression, whereas strong evoked bursting activity remains unchanged even with high-power Arch activation

span.label: the imaging tool is biased in one direction - SOM CELLS ARE KNOWN TO HAVE HIGH BASAL FIRING RATES, and TDTOMATO LABELING IN HIGH CONCENTRATIONS CAN CONTAMINATE THE FLUORESCENCE SIGNAL, so BOTH OF THESE CAVEATS COULD LEAD THIS TECHNIQUE TO UNDERESTIMATE NEURONAL FIRING RATES
span.quote: Two caveats to this approach are that SOM cells are known to have high basal firing rates, and TdTomato labeling in high concentrations can contaminate the fluorescence signal. Both of these caveats could lead this technique to underestimate neuronal firing rates

span.label: activating a cell that is normally switched off by the stimulus is not a mild intervention - in S1 SOM CELLS, WHICH ARE NORMALLY HYPERPOLARIZED BY SENSORY STIMULATION, OPTOGENETIC ACTIVATION WOULD PRODUCE HIGHLY UNNATURAL ACTIVITY
span.quote: In S1 SOM cells, for example, which are normally hyperpolarized by sensory stimulation, optogenetic activation would produce highly unnatural activity

span.label: THE CELLULAR AND SYNAPTIC EFFECTS OF SOM RELEASE IN CORTEX HAVE NOT BEEN STUDIED - the molecule the whole class is named after is unmeasured in the tissue the review is about
span.quote: The cellular and synaptic effects of SOM release in cortex have not been studied.

span.label: MANY OF THESE STUDIES ARE RELATIVELY OLD AND HAVE NOT BEEN REPLICATED RECENTLY, DESPITE BROAD INTEREST IN THE TOPIC
span.quote: However, it's worth noting that many of these studies are relatively old and have not been replicated recently, despite broad interest in the topic.

span.label: the optogenetic tools HAVE IMPORTANT LIMITATIONS THAT MUST BE CONSIDERED WHEN INTERPRETING THE RESULTS, because VARIABILITY IN ILLUMINATION INTENSITY AND DURATION, TRANSGENIC VS. VIRAL EXPRESSION, AND THE DETAILS OF SENSORY STIMULI OR TASK PARAMETERS CAN INTERACT IN COMPLEX WAYS EVEN IN THE SAME CORTICAL REGION
span.quote: Although new optogenetic tools have been indispensable in understanding the role of specific cell types in intact cortical circuits in vivo , they do have important limitations that must be considered when interpreting the results. Variability in illumination intensity and duration, transgenic vs. viral expression, and the details of sensory stimuli or task parameters can interact in complex ways that affect how neurons respond to optogenetic manipulation even in the same cortical region.

span.label: THE DISCREPANCY SO FAR HAS NOT BE INVESTIGATED AND COULD ARISE FROM EITHER DIFFERENCES IN RECORDING METHODS OR ANIMAL AGE
span.quote: But in slice recordings from younger animals, the waveform of SOM neurons is comparable in width to excitatory neurons (McGarry et al., 2010 ). This discrepancy so far has not be investigated and could arise from either differences in recording methods or animal age.

span.label: the firing-type names REGULAR SPIKING AND BURSTING, ORIGINALLY DESCRIBED FOR CORTICAL PYRAMIDAL NEURONS - and the review states the limit of the loan itself: ANALOGOUS BUT NOT IDENTICAL TO THOSE CLASSICALLY OBSERVED IN PYRAMIDAL NEURONS
span.quote: Regular spiking and bursting firing types were originally described for cortical pyramidal neurons (Connors et al., 1982 ), and it is important to note that the firing properties of RS or bursting SOM cells are analogous but not identical to those classically observed in pyramidal neurons.

span.label: the rebound-burst mechanism - REBOUND SPIKES/BURSTS ARE MEDIATED BY T-TYPE CALCIUM CHANNELS, SIMILAR TO THOSE FOUND IN THALAMIC RELAY NEURONS, and LIKE RELAY NEURONS, L5 LTS CELLS CAN FIRE IN EITHER TONIC OR BURSTING MODE
span.quote: These rebound spikes/bursts are mediated by T-type calcium channels, similar to those found in thalamic relay neurons (Goldberg et al., 2004 ; Ma et al., 2006 ). Like relay neurons, L5 LTS cells can fire in either tonic or bursting mode, depending on their membrane potential.

span.label: the 256 combinations cut down by the co-expression the literature reports as absent
span.quote: Thus there are 2 morphological types, 2 6 potential combinations of molecular markers, and 2 firing-property classes, leading to 256 possible subtypes of SOM cells

span.label: the disagreement between two labs checked against their methods before being read as a difference between cortical areas
span.quote: The difference between these findings may indicate different circuits in somatosensory and visual cortex, but it is important to note that these studies also used different methods. Xu et al. performed slice experiments using current injections in single SOM neurons and optogenetic suppression of SOM neurons, whereas Cottam et al. looked at neural firing rate in vivo in behaving animals with and without presentation of visual stimuli while optogenetically activating many SOM neurons. Considering that brain states can strongly affect neural activity, it is quite possible that the reported differences in the inhibitory contribution of L2/3 SOM cells to neighboring neurons could be explained by different cortical states and the number of SOM cells recruited.

span.label: the divisive-against-subtractive conflict traced to stimulation duration
span.quote: Importantly, one of these studies used brief activation (Wilson et al., 2012 ), whereas the other used prolonged activation (Lee et al., 2012 ). Brief SOM activation (which would result in less co-activation) produced a subtractive effect, whereas prolonged SOM activation (with more co-activation) produced a divisive effect

span.label: the two learning results, in opposite directions, separated by which layer and which synapse was counted
span.quote: These two results—fewer SOM synapses after motor learning, but more synapses after associative learning—appear at first glance to be contradictory. However, the decrease after motor learning was seen for L1 synapses onto L2/3 apical dendrites, whereas the increase after associative learning was seen in L4. The former are almost certainly synapses from Martinotti cells, which target PNs, whereas the relevant L4 SOM cells could be non-Martinotti cells that target PV interneurons in L4. The net effect of these changes could therefore be in the same direction

span.label: the sharpened-tuning result read against the spike threshold rather than against the inhibition
span.quote: These conflicting results can best be understood in the context of the “iceberg effect,” which refers to the idea that firing rates cannot go below zero (i.e., the water level), which hides the subthreshold tuning curve.

span.label: THE CATEGORY DOES NOT CARVE, AND THE REVIEW SAYS SO IN ITS OWN VOICE: THESE APPROACHES TYPICALLY PRODUCE PARTIALLY OVERLAPPING CATEGORIES, PRODUCING AN INEVITABLE TENSION BETWEEN THE TENDENCY TO BE A “LUMPER” OR A “SPLITTER.”
span.quote: These approaches typically produce partially overlapping categories, producing an inevitable tension between the tendency to be a “lumper” or a “splitter.”

span.label: AND THE UNCERTAINTY IS QUANTIFIED RATHER THAN HEDGED: THE TRUE NUMBER OF DISTINCT SUBTYPES OF SOM CELLS IS UNKNOWN, and it MOST LIKELY LIES SOMEWHERE BETWEEN 4 AND 100 SUBTYPES. A twenty-five-fold range on how many kinds of thing the name refers to, printed as the review's own estimate
span.quote: Thus while the true number of distinct subtypes of SOM cells is unknown, we estimate that it most likely lies somewhere between 4 and 100 subtypes.

span.label: the upper bound is a count of what has NOT BEEN RULED OUT, not of what has been seen: THESE ASSUMPTIONS ARE POORLY CONSTRAINED BY DATA BECAUSE MOST STUDIES HAVE MEASURED ONLY A SUBSET OF THESE CRITERIA, and ADDITIONAL DATA THAT FURTHER CONSTRAINS THE NUMBER OF POSSIBLE COMBINATIONS WOULD REDUCE THIS NUMBER
span.quote: Estimating such an upper bound requires several assumptions about whether classification criteria can vary independently (producing all possible combinations) or whether there are correlations that reduce the number of combinations. These assumptions are poorly constrained by data because most studies have measured only a subset of these criteria. In addition, we assume here that these criteria are static, although it's likely that some criteria could change over time.

span.label: ONE CRITERION CANNOT IDENTIFY THE CLASS: SOM-POSITIVE CELLS CAN ALSO EXHIBIT TONIC FAST SPIKING FIRING PROPERTIES AND PV-POSITIVE NEURONS CAN BE STUTTERING FAST SPIKING, WHICH INDICATES THAT DIFFERENT CELLS TYPES CAN HAVE SIMILAR FIRING PROPERTIES AND THUS THIS CRITERION ALONE CAN NOT BE USED TO RELIABLY IDENTIFY A SPECIFIC CELL TYPE
span.quote: In piriform cortex, SOM-positive cells can also exhibit tonic fast spiking firing properties and PV-positive neurons can be stuttering fast spiking, which indicates that different cells types can have similar firing properties and thus this criterion alone can not be used to reliably identify a specific cell type

span.label: AND THE SAME CRITERION CAN FAIL IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE: CLASSIFICATION OF SOM CELLS BASED ON FIRING PROPERTIES ALONE COULD LUMP TOGETHER DISTINCT CLASSES OR ERRONEOUSLY SPLIT A SINGLE CLASS, DEPENDING ON THE SAMPLE BEING STUDIED. Not a bias with a direction - a bias whose direction is set by whoever's cells you happen to have
span.quote: It seems likely that classification of SOM cells based on firing properties alone (such as the tendency to burst) could lump together distinct classes or erroneously split a single class, depending on the sample being studied.

span.label: A DISTINCTION THAT EXISTS IN THE TOOL AND NOT IN THE TISSUE: L4 SOM CELLS MAY BE A SINGLE POPULATION, WITH NO APPARENT FUNCTIONAL CORRELATES OF THEIR SEGREGATION INTO X94 AND NON-X94 CATEGORIES. The line drew the boundary; nothing measured since has found anything on either side of it
span.quote: Thus it appears that L4 SOM cells may be a single population, with no apparent functional correlates of their segregation into X94 and non-X94 categories

span.label: IT IS STILL NOT CLEAR WHETHER LTS AND BURSTING SOM CELLS FORM TWO DISTINCT CATEGORIES OR INSTEAD ARE A SINGLE CLASS THAT LIE ALONG A CONTINUUM - the question of whether two names name two things, left open in the review's own words
span.quote: It is still not clear whether LTS and bursting SOM cells form two distinct categories or instead are a single class that lie along a continuum.

span.label: and the disagreement may be nothing but vocabulary: DIFFERENT STUDIES HAVE ADOPTED DIFFERENT TERMINOLOGY (EITHER BURSTING OR LTS), AND REPORT SOMEWHAT DIFFERENT LAMINAR DISTRIBUTIONS, WHICH IS FURTHER COMPLICATED BY THE FACT THAT SOME STUDIES ARE IN RAT WHILE OTHERS ARE IN MOUSE
span.quote: Different studies have adopted different terminology (either bursting or LTS), and report somewhat different laminar distributions, which is further complicated by the fact that some studies are in rat while others are in mouse

span.label: THE CATEGORIES ARE NOT EVEN THE SAME ACROSS SPECIES: IN RATS PV, SOM, AND CALRETININ (CR) CELLS FORM NON-OVERLAPPING CATEGORIES, WHEREAS MICE SHOW OVERLAPPING EXPRESSION OF SOM AND CR. The same three names partition one animal and not the other
span.quote: These categories vary across species; in rats, for example, PV, SOM, and calretinin (CR) cells form non-overlapping categories (Gonchar and Burkhalter, 1997 ; Kawaguchi and Kubota, 1997 ), whereas mice show overlapping expression of SOM and CR

span.label: THE INCLUSION IS ONE-WAY AND THE REVIEW SAYS BOTH HALVES: ALL MARTINOTTI CELLS ARE SOM-POSITIVE, HOWEVER NOT ALL SOM-POSITIVE CELLS ARE MARTINOTTI CELLS - the exact shape a `is-a` edge needs and almost never gets
span.quote: All Martinotti cells are SOM-positive, however not all SOM-positive cells are Martinotti cells.

span.label: the same one-way shape, denied in both directions for the other class: NOT ALL PV CELLS ARE FS CELLS, AND NOT ALL FS CELLS ARE PV CELLS. A molecular name and a physiological name that are used interchangeably and are not the same set
span.quote: However, not all PV cells are FS cells, and not all FS cells are PV cells

span.label: THE TOOL THAT MAKES THE CLASS VISIBLE LEAKS INTO THE CLASS IT IS DEFINED AGAINST: AT LEAST ONE SOM-CRE LINE ALSO ERRONEOUSLY MARKS A SMALL SUBSET (6-10%) OF FAST SPIKING PV NEURONS
span.quote: It is important to note that at least one SOM-Cre line (Taniguchi et al., 2011 ; Jax Stock No. 013044) also erroneously marks a small subset (6–10%) of fast spiking PV neurons

span.label: and the census is biased by the same tool: BECAUSE THEY LABEL ONLY SUBSETS OF SOM CELLS, ONE MUST BE CAREFUL NOT TO INFER RELATIVE PROPORTIONS OF SOM SUBTYPES FROM STUDIES USING THESE LINES
span.quote: But because they label only subsets of SOM cells, one must be careful not to infer relative proportions of SOM subtypes from studies using these lines.

span.label: THE PROPERTY BELONGS TO THE INTERACTION, NOT TO THE CELL TYPE: WHETHER GAIN CONTROL IS DIVISIVE OR SUBTRACTIVE IS DYNAMIC AND STIMULUS-DEPENDENT, RATHER THAN A FIXED PROPERTY OF A GIVEN CELL TYPE. Every tag of the form `SOM provides subtractive inhibition` is therefore true only of a condition, and the condition is not in the tag
span.quote: This illustrates that whether gain control is divisive or subtractive is dynamic and stimulus-dependent, rather than a fixed property of a given cell type.

span.label: and it may not belong to the interneuron at all: THESE FORMS OF GAIN CONTROL MAY NOT BE DETERMINED BY THE TYPE OF INTERNEURON, BUT RATHER BY INTRINSIC PROPERTIES OF A TARGET NEURON. The property is attributed to the wrong cell
span.quote: This suggests that these forms of gain control may not be determined by the type of interneuron, but rather by intrinsic properties of a target neuron

span.label: A MEASUREMENT FLOOR THAT MANUFACTURES THE RESULT: FIRING RATES CANNOT GO BELOW ZERO (I.E., THE WATER LEVEL), WHICH HIDES THE SUBTHRESHOLD TUNING CURVE - so STRONGER SUPPRESSION OF PN SPIKING CAN NARROW TUNING CURVES, EVEN WITH PURELY DIVISIVE INHIBITION
span.quote: These conflicting results can best be understood in the context of the “iceberg effect,” which refers to the idea that firing rates cannot go below zero (i.e., the water level), which hides the subthreshold tuning curve.

span.label: which the review turns into a rule about the method: INFERRING THE PRESENCE OF DIVISIVE OR SUBTRACTIVE INHIBITION FROM OPTOGENETIC MANIPULATIONS CAN BE PROBLEMATIC
span.quote: These studies illustrate that inferring the presence of divisive or subtractive inhibition from optogenetic manipulations can be problematic

span.label: A CATEGORY BORROWED FROM ANOTHER CELL TYPE, WITH THE NON-IDENTITY STATED: REGULAR SPIKING AND BURSTING FIRING TYPES WERE ORIGINALLY DESCRIBED FOR CORTICAL PYRAMIDAL NEURONS, and THE FIRING PROPERTIES OF RS OR BURSTING SOM CELLS ARE ANALOGOUS BUT NOT IDENTICAL TO THOSE CLASSICALLY OBSERVED IN PYRAMIDAL NEURONS
span.quote: Regular spiking and bursting firing types were originally described for cortical pyramidal neurons (Connors et al., 1982 ), and it is important to note that the firing properties of RS or bursting SOM cells are analogous but not identical to those classically observed in pyramidal neurons.

span.label: the same paper suppressing SOM and REDUCING adaptation, read the other way round: SUPPRESSION OF SOM NEURONS REDUCES STIMULUS-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION IN OTHER CORTICAL NEURONS, INCREASING PN RESPONSES TO THE FREQUENT TONE - and SOM CELLS CONTRIBUTE TO STIMULUS-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION, EVEN WHILE EXPERIENCING STIMULUS-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION THEMSELVES
span.quote: Suppression of SOM neurons reduces stimulus-specific adaptation in other cortical neurons, increasing PN responses to the frequent tone. Thus SOM cells contribute to stimulus-specific adaptation, even while experiencing stimulus-specific adaptation themselves

span.label: and the same cells move the opposite way in the neighboring paradigm: THIS INCREASE IN SOM RESPONSIVENESS CONTRASTS WITH THE DECREASED SOM RESPONSIVENESS DURING STIMULUS-SPECIFIC ADAPTATION
span.quote: Tone-evoked responses in L2/3 SOM cells are increased as both PN and PV cell responses are decreased, suggested that SOM cells mediate the habituation in other cortical neurons. This increase in SOM responsiveness contrasts with the decreased SOM responsiveness during stimulus-specific adaptation.

span.label: THE CLASS CANNOT BE PERTURBED ALONE: IT IS VIRTUALLY IMPOSSIBLE TO PERTURB THE ACTIVITY OF THE SOM NETWORK WITHOUT CHANGING FIRING PATTERNS IN OTHER INHIBITORY NEURONS, WHICH MAY LEAD TO CONFLICTING AND MISLEADING RESULTS
span.quote: Lastly, high levels of interconnectivity in cortical circuits make it challenging to study the effects of only a single interneuron subtype. In particular, it is virtually impossible to perturb the activity of the SOM network without changing firing patterns in other inhibitory neurons, which may lead to conflicting and misleading results

span.label: and the review's closing instruction to its own readers: IT IS IMPORTANT TO REMEMBER THAT SOM CELLS ARE NOT A SINGLE POPULATION, BUT RATHER CONSIST OF SEVERAL DISTINCT CLASSES OF INHIBITORY CELLS
span.quote: It is important to remember that SOM cells are not a single population, but rather consist of several distinct classes of inhibitory cells

span.label: THE NAME IS ALSO A MOLECULE: SOMATOSTATIN IS NOT JUST A CELL-TYPE SPECIFIC MARKER, BUT ALSO AN INHIBITORY 14-AMINO-ACID NEUROPEPTIDE RELEASED BY THE SUBSET OF GABAERGIC NEURONS THAT EXPRESS THE SOMATOSTATIN GENE - one word doing duty as a label and as a substance
span.quote: Somatostatin is not just a cell-type specific marker, but also an inhibitory 14-amino-acid neuropeptide released by the subset of GABAergic neurons that express the somatostatin gene.

span.label: and what that substance does where the review is set is not known: THE CELLULAR AND SYNAPTIC EFFECTS OF SOM RELEASE IN CORTEX HAVE NOT BEEN STUDIED
span.quote: The cellular and synaptic effects of SOM release in cortex have not been studied.

span.label: the same class behaving oppositely in one sensory system: IN BARREL CORTEX SOM CELLS ARE SUPPRESSED DURING STIMULUS PRESENTATION, AND THUS ARE ANTI-CORRELATED WITH NETWORK ACTIVITY, A FEATURE WHICH HAS NOT BEEN OBSERVED IN OTHER SENSORY REGIONS
span.quote: Interestingly, in barrel cortex SOM cells are suppressed during stimulus presentation, and thus are anti-correlated with network activity, a feature which has not been observed in other sensory regions

span.label: reconciles → Xu et al. against Cottam et al. on how much L2/3 SOM cells inhibit other inhibitory cells
span.quote: The difference between these findings may indicate different circuits in somatosensory and visual cortex, but it is important to note that these studies also used different methods. Xu et al. performed slice experiments using current injections in single SOM neurons and optogenetic suppression of SOM neurons, whereas Cottam et al. looked at neural firing rate in vivo in behaving animals with and without presentation of visual stimuli while optogenetically activating many SOM neurons. Considering that brain states can strongly affect neural activity, it is quite possible that the reported differences in the inhibitory contribution of L2/3 SOM cells to neighboring neurons could be explained by different cortical states and the number of SOM cells recruited.

span.label: reconciles → Wilson et al. 2012 against Lee et al. 2012 on whether SOM activation sharpens orientation tuning
span.quote: In visual cortex, conflicting results have been reported for activation of SOM cells. One study found that SOM activation sharpened PN orientation tuning, consistent with subtractive inhibition (Wilson et al., 2012 ), whereas a similar study reported that SOM activation reduced PN spiking without any effect on tuning, consistent with divisive inhibition (Lee et al., 2012 ). A key to reconciling these disparate results may lie in the relative timing, size, and durations of sensory and optogenetic stimulation.

span.label: reconciles → fewer SOM synapses after motor learning against more synapses after associative learning
span.quote: These two results—fewer SOM synapses after motor learning, but more synapses after associative learning—appear at first glance to be contradictory. However, the decrease after motor learning was seen for L1 synapses onto L2/3 apical dendrites, whereas the increase after associative learning was seen in L4. The former are almost certainly synapses from Martinotti cells, which target PNs, whereas the relevant L4 SOM cells could be non-Martinotti cells that target PV interneurons in L4. The net effect of these changes could therefore be in the same direction

span.label: critiques → inferring divisive or subtractive inhibition from optogenetic manipulation
span.quote: These studies illustrate that inferring the presence of divisive or subtractive inhibition from optogenetic manipulations can be problematic

span.label: builds-on → Natan et al. 2015, that SOM cells contribute to stimulus-specific adaptation while adapting themselves
span.quote: Suppression of SOM neurons reduces stimulus-specific adaptation in other cortical neurons, increasing PN responses to the frequent tone. Thus SOM cells contribute to stimulus-specific adaptation, even while experiencing stimulus-specific adaptation themselves

span.label: qualifies → classification of SOM cells by firing properties
span.quote: It seems likely that classification of SOM cells based on firing properties alone (such as the tendency to burst) could lump together distinct classes or erroneously split a single class, depending on the sample being studied.

span.label: Martinotti —is-a→ SOM
span.quote: All Martinotti cells are SOM-positive, however not all SOM-positive cells are Martinotti cells.

span.label: SOM —is-a→ interneuron
span.quote: Cortical inhibitory neurons exhibit remarkable diversity in their morphology, connectivity, and synaptic properties. Here, we review the function of somatostatin-expressing (SOM) inhibitory interneurons, focusing largely on sensory cortex. SOM neurons also comprise a number of subpopulations that can be distinguished by their morphology, input and output connectivity, laminar location, firing properties, and expression of molecular markers.

span.label: SOM —part-of→ cortex
span.quote: In this review, we focus on SOM cells in cerebral cortex, with an emphasis on mice.

span.label: subtype —part-of→ SOM
span.quote: Thus while the true number of distinct subtypes of SOM cells is unknown, we estimate that it most likely lies somewhere between 4 and 100 subtypes.

span.label: SOM —distinct-from→ PV
span.quote: In piriform cortex, SOM-positive cells can also exhibit tonic fast spiking firing properties and PV-positive neurons can be stuttering fast spiking, which indicates that different cells types can have similar firing properties and thus this criterion alone can not be used to reliably identify a specific cell type

span.label: class —operationalised-as→ firing properties
